title: Open model platforms: Hugging Face Hub

opening.headline: Learn how to read Hugging Face Hub's model cards to see if you can use public models and datasets that anyone can download, and what their limitations are.
body: There are many publicly available AI models and datasets on the Internet. The fact that it is public does not mean that you can use it as you please, nor does it mean that it is suitable for your work. You can use it safely by knowing what it is made for, under what conditions it can be used, and what it is not good at.

In this class, we will first look at the configuration of Hugging Face Hub, which is a collection of public models, datasets, and demo apps. Next, learn how to read what the model card and dataset card consist of, and organize the confirmation sequence in the case of selecting model candidates for in-house document classification.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the purpose of open models, datasets, and demo platforms
Can distinguish between limitations and bias information of model cards

screens.title: The revealed model, can I use it or trust it?
screens.lead: We are in a situation where we want to use an open model for work. Read below and think about what questions you need to ask.

visual.alt: A scene with three speech bubbles surrounding the public model card in the center asking about license, limitations, and bias.

paragraphs: AI models and datasets are available on the Internet for anyone to download. If you find a model that seems to perform well, you'll want to try it out at work right away.

But just because it's public doesn't mean you can use it as you please. Each model has different terms of use, and some require approval for access. Also, just because it works well in the demo does not guarantee that it will be suitable for my job.
To use it safely, you need to know what it was made for, how it was evaluated, and what it cannot do. Today we look at how to read this information in the Hugging Face Hub.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Will a model that works well in the demo work well in my job? By the end of the lesson, you will be able to answer this question with the necessary checks.

screens.outro: First, let's recall our experience reading model cards.

screens.title: Have you ever read the model card?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever read a model card?
items.answer: People often choose models based solely on their name and popularity. The model card is the manual for that model, so you need to get into the habit of reading it before using it for work. Although it may seem long at first, you only need to find and read a few items.

items.prompt: If you read it, which did you find most helpful?
items.answer: Writing down the purpose and limitations will be the most helpful in making a decision. Because it says there what you can and shouldn't do with this model.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a public model and a service operated by a provider?
items.answer: The service provider's service has usage policies and instructions and is also in charge of operation. Since I use the public model myself, I am also responsible for reading the conditions and checking the limits.

screens.outro: Let’s start by looking at what the Hub is structured like.

screens.title: Configuration of Hugging Face Hub
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the three resources and assistive features found in the Hub.

tabs.label: What is Hub?
tabs.body: Hugging Face Hub is a collaborative platform that collects publicly available models, datasets, and apps. According to the documentation, it hosts over 2 million models, 1.5 million datasets, and 1.5 million apps. In addition to public data, it is also used for internal team and private use. Data is stored in a version-controlled repository, allowing change history and comparison functions.

tabs.label: Models
tabs.body: Models is a place to upload and download models for language, text, vision, and audio work. You can search by task type and language, and it is linked to several libraries. Importantly, each model repository has a model card. The document explains that model cards inform the limitations and biases of each model to ensure responsible use.

tabs.label: Datasets
tabs.body: Datasets are a collection of public datasets from various fields and types. The document introduces that there are more than 500,000 public datasets spanning over 8,000 languages. Datasets come with a dataset card that describes their composition and sources, and there's also a Data Studio that lets you explore the data directly in your browser.

tabs.label: Spaces
tabs.body: Spaces hosts demo apps that let you try out models right away. You can upload apps created with Gradio and Streamlit, static HTML pages, and Docker-based apps. It's convenient for showing your results to stakeholders, but the fact that a demo works doesn't mean it's right for your job.

tabs.label: access control
tabs.body: The Hub has security and access control features. Features such as user access tokens, organizational access control, and malware scanning are introduced. Additionally, some models and datasets are provided in a gated manner that places conditions on access.

screens.outro: Now that you know the configuration of the Hub, let's see how to read the most important document: the model card.

screens.title: Composition of model card and dataset card
screens.lead: Selecting the number markers in the picture will reveal what each item on the model card says and how it should be read.

visual.alt: Model card screen Illustration of model and purpose, license, evaluation results, limitations and biases, and dataset cards with numbered markers.
labels: Intended use and type of work
Under what conditions can it be used?
By what standard was it measured?
What I'm not good at and what I'm biased towards

markers.label: Use
markers.title: Intended use and type of work
markers.body: This is the part that states what task the model was created for. You'll also see metadata here, such as task type and supported languages. The first thing to check is whether my work fits this purpose. If you are dealing with a Korean document and there is no Korean in the supported language, it is safe to exclude it as a candidate.

markers.label: license
markers.title: Under what conditions can it be used?
markers.body: Even for publicly available models, conditions of use are set. Check conditions such as whether business or commercial use is permitted and whether the results must be made public. If terms are unclear, contact your organization's responsible department before use.

markers.label: Evaluation results
markers.title: By what standard was it measured?
markers.body: The evaluation results show the model's performance. What data and criteria it is measured by is more important than the number itself. It is difficult to believe the results if they are measured using data that is different from the nature of my work.

markers.label: Limitations and Bias
markers.title: What I'm not good at and what I'm biased towards
markers.body: The Hub document explains that model cards inform you of the limitations and biases of your model for responsible use. This section reads about weak language, groups, and when not to use it. If limitations and biases are unwritten or vague, that in itself is a red flag.

markers.label: Dataset Card
markers.title: Source and organization of data
markers.body: The dataset card explains where the data comes from and how it is organized. Whether the data contains human information or whether certain groups are missing also leads to model bias. Reading it together with the model card will make your judgment more accurate.

screens.outro: Now that we know the items, let's take an example of the confirmation order for an actual candidate.

screens.title: Commentary: Check licenses and limits when choosing a public model
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step the process of comparing two public model candidates for in-house document classification. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: There are two public model candidates for classifying company documents by business type. The candidate has a lot of downloads and the demo works well. Candidate I is less well-known, but the model card is detailed.

steps.title: Step 1: Check your license
steps.body: First, check if business use is permitted. Unusable models cannot be candidates no matter how good their performance is, so they are filtered out first in this step.

steps.title: Step 2: Verify that it is suitable for its intended use
steps.body: Verify that the card's intended use and supported language match my work. A model built for document classification and a model built for conversation cannot be evaluated in the same way.

steps.title: Step 3: Check the criteria for evaluation results
steps.body: Check what data and criteria the evaluation results were measured against. The key is whether it is measured using data that is similar in nature to our document. If the evaluation information is empty, you must first apply it to a small number of documents and make your own judgment.

steps.title: Step 4: Read the limitations, biases, and access conditions
steps.body: In the limitations and biases section of the card, read for weak language or when not to use it. If it is a gated model that requires access approval, we also check the access conditions and consider whether in-house documents can be processed without sending them externally.

steps.title: Collect verification results in a table
steps.body: The results of the four steps are recorded in a table for each candidate. The differences between the two candidates can be seen at a glance by columns of licensure availability, fit for use, appropriateness of evaluation criteria, known limitations, and access conditions. Blank fields have not been checked yet, so mark them separately.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: The number of downloads and the completeness of the demo are not the basis for judgment. By tabulating the results in the order of license, purpose, evaluation criteria, and limitations, you can fairly compare the two candidates. If a card clearly states detailed candidates and limitations, it may be a more reliable choice.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the confirmation order, let's put it all together on one page.

screens.title: The model card is a document that reads the limits.
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard. Please read this while thinking about the order in which you will look when choosing a model in the future.

paragraphs: Hugging Face Hub is a collection of public models, datasets, and demo spaces. The advantage is that there is a lot of data and it is easy to access, but the responsibility of the person choosing it also increases.

The model card is not a promotional document, but rather a document that reads usage, license, evaluation, limitations and biases. If limitations and biases are not written or are vague, that fact itself should be taken as a red flag. Read the dataset card as well, as it tells you where the data comes from and how it is organized.

The order of verification before use is license, purpose, evaluation criteria, limitations and biases, and access conditions. Even if the demo works well, you need to check separately whether it is suitable for your work. Lastly, remember that the public model, unlike the provider's service, requires you to take responsibility for both operation and responsibility. As I personally decide how to use it and in what environment, the number of things to check also increases. If you start with this knowledge, the open model is a great starting point.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Open only means that it can be accessed, not that it can be used freely. Please check the license and limitations before using.

glossary.def: A platform to upload, find, and share public AI models, datasets, and apps.
A document that describes the model's purpose, evaluation, limitations and biases, and licensing.
A document that explains the source and organization of data.
This is a space that hosts demo apps where you can try out the model right away.
This model can be downloaded only if access conditions are met.

misconceptions.myth: If it is public, you can use it freely.
misconceptions.fact: Each model has different licensing and access conditions. You should check the terms of use before using it for work.

misconceptions.myth: A model card is a promotional document.
misconceptions.fact: The model card is also a document that indicates the limitations and biases of the model. You need to read for the weak points, not just the good points.

misconceptions.myth: If the demo runs well, it works well for the job.
misconceptions.fact: A demo simply shows the operation in action on a given example. You must separately check whether the purpose and evaluation criteria fit your work.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The Hub is a collection of public models, datasets, and demos.
A model card is a document that reads its purpose, limitations, and biases.
Check the license and access conditions first.
Even if the demo runs well, I check separately whether it is suitable for my work.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: If you were to choose a public model, what would you look at first on the model card?

checks.q: What is the best combination of items to check on the model card of a public model?
options: Intended use, license, evaluation results, limitations and biases
Number of downloads and length of model name
Photo and introduction of the person who uploaded the model
Screen color and number of demo apps
checks.explain: The card reads purpose, license, evaluation results, unintended uses and limitations, and bias. If limits and biases are vaguely stated, that in itself is a red flag.

wrong.1: Popularity indicators do not tell you whether something is usable or trustworthy.
wrong.2: The author's introduction does not provide information about the conditions of use and limitations of the model.
wrong.3: Appearance has nothing to do with fitness for the job.

checks.intro: Check yourself how to read the model card you just saw. Results are not recorded, and commentary appears immediately after you select an option.

checks.q: Lay out public model candidates for in-house document classification in the order you look at them.
items: Check if your license allows for business use
Check whether the intended use of the card fits my work
Check what data and standards the evaluation results were measured against.
Check limits, bias, and access conditions if it is a gated model.
checks.explain: We first filter out availability, then use, rating, and limitations.
checks.intro: Think about the order in which you would look at the public model candidates and arrange them. Results are not recorded.
